slides.title: Going Solar at Home
slides.subtitle: A practical guide for homeowners
slides.notes: Welcome everyone. Today we'll walk through what going solar means for your home, from understanding the basics to maintaining a system after installation. Feel free to ask questions at any point.

items: How a home solar system works
Is your home a good fit?
slides.notes: Here's our roadmap for the session. We'll start with the reasons homeowners go solar, then cover how systems work, whether your roof is suitable, what it costs, how to pick an installer, and what happens after installation.

slides.title: Homeowners go solar for three main reasons
slides.notes: Most homeowners are motivated by a combination of these three factors. For some, savings dominate; for others, it's about resilience during outages or personal values. Your own priorities will shape which system and financing make sense.

slides.title: A home solar system works in four steps

steps.title: Sunlight hits panels
steps.text: Panels on your roof convert sunlight into direct current electricity.

steps.title: Inverter converts power
steps.text: The inverter turns DC electricity into the AC power your home uses.

steps.title: Home uses the electricity
steps.text: Your appliances run on solar power first, before drawing from the grid.

steps.title: Excess is exported or stored
steps.text: Surplus power goes to a battery or back to the grid, depending on your setup.

slides.notes: The flow is simple: panels generate DC power, the inverter converts it to AC, your home uses it, and any surplus is stored in a battery or fed back to the grid. Net metering rules in your area determine how exported power is credited.

slides.title: A good solar home has sun, space and a sound roof

left.heading: What helps
bullets: Little shade from trees or buildings

right.heading: What complicates things
bullets: Heavy shading for much of the day

slides.notes: Not every home is equally suited to solar. Orientation, shading and roof condition matter most. If your roof needs replacing soon, it's often cheaper to do that before installing panels. A site assessment will confirm your situation.

slides.title: Buy, finance or lease: three ways to go solar

left.heading: Buy outright
bullets: You own the system and incentives

right.heading: Loan or lease
bullets: Leasing means the installer owns the system

slides.notes: Buying outright maximises long-term savings but requires capital. Loans spread the cost while you keep ownership benefits. Leases and power purchase agreements lower the barrier but typically offer smaller savings since you don't own the equipment. Compare total costs over the full term, not just monthly payments.

slides.title: From first call to first kilowatt: the installation journey

steps.title: Site assessment
steps.text: An installer inspects your roof, shading and electrical panel.

steps.title: Design and quote
steps.text: You receive a system design, production estimate and pricing.

steps.title: Permits and approvals
steps.text: The installer handles local permits and utility interconnection.

steps.title: Installation day
steps.text: Most residential installs take one to three days.

steps.title: Inspection and activation
steps.text: Final inspection, utility permission, then your system goes live.

slides.notes: The timeline is mostly waiting on permits and utility approval rather than the physical work itself. Ask your installer for a realistic schedule upfront. Once activated, monitoring apps let you track production from day one.

slides.title: Choose an installer the way you'd choose any contractor
bullets: Read reviews and ask for references
Compare warranties on panels and workmanship
slides.notes: Quotes can vary widely for the same equipment, so comparison shopping pays off. Verify credentials and ask who will actually perform the work. A reputable installer will welcome questions and never pressure you to sign on the spot.

slides.title: Solar systems need little, but not zero, attention
bullets: Panels are typically cleaned by rain
Keep an eye on inverter status lights
Schedule a professional check every few years
Warranties often run 20-25 years on panels
slides.notes: Maintenance is minimal: rain handles most cleaning, and monitoring apps flag problems early. The inverter is the component most likely to need replacement within the system's life. Keep your warranty documents and installer contact details handy.

slides.title: Thank you
slides.subtitle: Ready to explore solar for your home? Start with a site assessment.
slides.notes: Thank you for your time. Your next step is simple: book a site assessment with a reputable installer and compare quotes. We're happy to answer any remaining questions now.
